summary:
Curaçao is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It holds full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

Same-sex sexual activity, both male and female, is legal in Curaçao. The age of consent is 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Curaçao since the 12 July 2024 ruling of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upholding the Appeals Court decision that barring such marriages discriminated on the basis of sexual orientation.

Before that ruling, Curaçao was required as part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to recognise as valid same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. Same-sex couples could not marry in Curaçao itself and no civil unions or other forms of recognition were available.

The Criminal Code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including "heterosexual or homosexual orientation". Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference which has the purpose or effect of impacting or affecting recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties including fines and imprisonment of up to one year.

The European Court of Human Rights has jurisdiction over Curaçao. In Oliari and Others v. Italy in August 2015 it held that providing no legal recognition to same-sex couples is discriminatory.

In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that lesbian, gay and bisexual people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights without delay, and a package of rights requests was delivered to ministers in The Hague. The agreement records a political commitment to equal treatment. It does not create an immediately enforceable right that a visitor can invoke at a border or in a local court.

Curaçao Commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly backed equal rights for everyone in April 2015. Her party colleague Winifred Raveneau opposed that position and had forced the 2013 Curaçao Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel through a last-minute exceptionally strict permit requirement.

Curaçao opened an LGBT Pink House centre in 2010. Curaçao Gay Pride representative Frank Holtslag has cited the International Gay and Lesbian Travel Association award describing Curaçao as most gay welcoming in the region.
tangentialFactors:
Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships on 8 September 2016. That measure is a comparator from elsewhere in the Kingdom of the Netherlands and is not Curaçao law.

GlobalGayz described Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao as quiet nests of gay-friendliness inside the Kingdom of the Netherlands and identified Curaçao with Sint Maarten and Aruba as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom.
localsOnly: A bill to allow same-sex couples to marry was submitted to the Estates of Curaçao on 4 June 2019. It was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support.
